body: You're in the driveway with a number on your phone that has a comma in it. The quote says the meter, probably the panel, maybe some of the wiring. You can't see inside the wall, and you can't tell whether any of it is real.
A warm outlet. A breaker that won't stay on. An inspector's note. You don't know a small fix from an expensive one, and the person quoting you knows that.
So you wait, or you sign. Neither feels good.

sections.heading: Electrical Repair: Find the Cause, Fix That

We trace it to the source, fix that and test the work before we leave. If we find a second problem on the way, we show you and you decide.
A warm outlet, a buzzing sound or a burning smell is a different story. That's a loose or failing connection. Stop using it and call us.

sections.heading: Why Things Stop Working
body: Electrical problems feel random. They aren't. Every dead outlet and tripping breaker has a cause, and it's usually one of a short list.
A connection has worked loose. A device has worn out. A circuit is carrying more than it was built for. Or a wire was run wrong years ago and the house has been getting by.
The fix depends on which one it is. Sometimes the cause isn't in the house at all. If the trouble is on the utility's side of the meter, the first call is to Evergy.

sections.heading: Breakers That Trip
body: A breaker is a safety device. It trips to stop a circuit from overheating, and it trips for one of three reasons: the circuit is overloaded, there's a short, or current is leaking to ground.
Overload is the common one, like a space heater and a hair dryer on the same circuit. Unplug what was running, reset the breaker once, and if it holds, you've probably found your overload.
If it trips again right away, or feels warm, or won't reset at all, stop and call us. Don't keep flipping it.

sections.heading: Outlets and Switches That Don't Work
body: These are the usual causes when something goes dead, and what we do about each.

items.title: The outlet itself has worn out
items.text: The device inside wears with use, and a loose wire behind it can stop it working. We replace the device and check the connection.

items.title: A ground-fault outlet tripped somewhere else
items.text: Bathroom, garage and outdoor outlets are the usual places. One tripped outlet can cut power to everything downstream of it.

items.title: A switch has worn out
items.text: The contacts inside wear, and eventually the light works when it wants to. A new switch fixes it.

items.title: A wire has come loose
items.text: Loose connections cause dead outlets, flicker and heat. We find which one and tighten or replace it.

sections.heading: When an Old Panel Is a Safety Problem
body: A panel that works isn't always a panel that's safe. These are the signs to look for.
list: A fuse box. Fuses are older technology and often mean a small service and old wiring.
Federal Pacific Stab-Lok or Zinsco breakers, two brands known to fail to trip.
Rust, scorch marks or a burning smell at the panel.
Two wires under one breaker, when most are built for one.
No open slots, so the next circuit gets squeezed in where it shouldn't.
A service too small for the house, now running central air, an electric range or an EV charger.

image.alt: Open home electrical panel with rows of breakers

sections.heading: We Start by Looking at What You Have
body: A panel replacement is a real expense, so we look at what you have first. Sometimes the answer is a new breaker or a repaired connection. Sometimes the panel is fine and the problem is on the utility's side of the meter.
If none of the signs above describes your panel, it may be fine as it is, and we'll say so.

items.title: A permit and an inspection
items.text: A panel upgrade needs a permit, and the city inspects the work before it's signed off.

items.title: The power company
items.text: Evergy disconnects your service so the panel can be swapped, then reconnects it.

items.title: The swap
items.text: The old panel comes out, the new one goes in, and every circuit is connected and tested. A new panel is often 200 amps.

items.title: Sometimes more
items.text: An old meter base or service mast may need replacing at the same time, depending on your house.

items.title: Labeling
items.text: A finished panel should have every circuit labeled, so you know what each breaker controls.

sections.heading: How Long the Power Is Off
body: A panel upgrade usually takes a day, with the power off for part of it.
Ask for the length of the outage when you get the quote, so you can plan around it. Tell us if anyone in the house depends on power for medical equipment.

sections.heading: A Sub-Panel for the Garage, Shop or a New Load
body: You don't always need a whole new main panel. If the garage, the workshop or an addition needs more power, a sub-panel feeds a new set of circuits from the main one, as long as the main service can carry the load.
An EV charger, a welder or a compressor adds load, so the main panel gets checked first.

sections.heading: Older Houses
body: Open the door on an old panel and you may find faded pencil, or no labels at all. Every breaker is a guess, and that's when the wrong one gets switched off.
A panel upgrade is the chance to fix that, and to bring an older house's wiring up to what it now has to carry.
